name: Theertha International Artists' Collective
overview: Artist-led non-profit arts organisation in Colombo that runs residencies, workshops, exhibitions and publications (Khoj Studios, Mediamatic).
Founded in 2000 by 11 visual artists (Khoj Studios). Mediamatic's listing says it is run by 17 visual artists.

Started its own exhibition space, the Red Dot Gallery, in 2007 to show experimental and contemporary art (Khoj Studios, artscollaboratory.org). The Sunday Times (30 September 2007) places the gallery at 36A Baddegana Road South, Pita Kotte.
funding_verdict: Theertha: artist-led non-profit: participant in the Arts Collaboratory programme of the Dutch foundations Hivos and DOEN, plus self-sponsored residency fees

name: The Muse Multi Studios
overview: Describes itself as an "integrative regional artistic organisation" founded in Khartoum. It lists Bait Alnisa, Muse Gallery and the Sudan Art Archive as its studios (Muse website).

Founded in 2019 by the Sudanese artist and curator Reem Aljeally, who is founder and director. Muse Gallery, its first space, opened in Khartoum in September 2022 (Muse website). OkayAfrica (Elizabeth Okwach, 6 July 2022) describes it as "an enterprise that works towards building a platform for the local art community".
It says the gallery is "temporarily closed due to the tragic war events" in Sudan since April 2023.
funding_verdict: The Muse Multi Studios: small-grant funded: Culture Resource's Abbara Program (2022) and an Australian-supported fellowship

name: Konsthall C
overview: Non-profit exhibition space in a former communal laundry at Cigarrvägen 14 in Hökarängen, a suburb of southern Stockholm (e-flux listing; e-flux call for applications, 20 May 2023).
Began in 2004 as a public artwork by the artist Per Hasselberg, made with local community organisations (Creative Time Summit page).

It describes itself as "an art gallery, public artwork, and an experiment in urban renewal" that has grown from an artist-run project space into "an established contemporary art platform" (e-flux call, 2023).
funding_verdict: Konsthall C: public support: Region Stockholm, the City of Stockholm and the Swedish Arts Council

name: Magasin III
overview: Private museum for contemporary art with its collection in Stockholm's Freeport (Frihamnsgatan 28) and a branch, Magasin III Jaffa, at 34 Olei Zion in Jaffa, Tel Aviv.
Founded in 1987 by David Neuman and Robert Weil. It began as Magasin 3 Stockholm Konsthall, with no collection, and later became Magasin III Museum for Contemporary Art (stated by the museum).

Building: a 1920s warehouse in the Freeport, an industrial space (Weil Foundation). The architecture firm DinellJohansson reworked the entrance and added a library and seminar room for the reopening after the 2017 closure (e-flux). The Jaffa space is 180 square metres (Kunstkritikk).
funding_verdict: Magasin III: self-funded by its owner family: the Robert Weil Family Foundation, paid for by the family-owned investment company Proventus

press_items.title: Karl Lydén, "- No. Or rather, yes and no" (2018)
interview with David Neuman and Tessa Praun, "Collecting for the private museum" (2023)

name: Tensta konsthall
overview: Contemporary art centre at Taxingegränd 10 in Tensta, northwest Stockholm, in "formerly unused storage space underneath Tensta Shopping Mall", about 700 square metres at Taxingeplan (tenstakonsthall.se, Wikipedia).

Founded in 1998 as a grassroots initiative, partly in connection with Stockholm being Capital of Europe that year (stated by the space). Wikipedia names the artist and social worker Gregor Wroblewski as founder.
Directors after him: Rodrigo Mallea Lira, Ylva Ogland and Jelena Rundqvist, William Easton, Maria Lind, and Cecilia Widenheim (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Tensta konsthall: mainly public: the City of Stockholm, the Swedish Arts Council and Region Stockholm
wider_context: 2012: "Abstract Possible: The Stockholm Synergies" (12 January to 22 April 2012, curated by Maria Lind) put its economic strand in the auction house Bukowskis, which Kunstkritikk says the Lundin family owns. Works sold there at fixed prices (e-flux, Judith Schwarzbart, 3 April 2012).

Kunstkritikk (Frans Josef Petersson, 28 February 2012) reports a debate at the konsthall in which Lundin Petroleum and the Lundin family were named. Artist Andreas Gedin said Lundin Petroleum had faced criticism from Amnesty and the UN. The article does not mention Sudan. Lind said "The project is not about taking a position" and, pressed, that "if the charges leveled against Lundin are true they are serious, and they should be condemned".
Unverified: that Lind's fee and the sales proceeds were withheld from the public, from Petersson in Kunstkritikk, a critical commentary. The pieces read give no amounts.
Bukowskis was a show partner and sales venue, not a listed funder of the konsthall.

press_items.title: Frans Josef Petersson, "Critical Collapse at Tensta Konsthall" (2012)
Judith Schwarzbart, "Abstract Possible: The Stockholm Synergies" (2012)

name: Ein Haus WOBA
overview: Row house at Im Surinam 126 in the WOBA estate, hidden between the railway embankments behind the Badischer Bahnhof in Basel. Bus 36 to Lange Erlen, then 200 m on foot (association's site).

Built in 1930 for the first Swiss housing exhibition (WOBA) by the architects Paul Artaria and Hans Schmidt. About 45 m² of living space for a family of four, and the last house of the estate with a largely original interior (association's site).
Verein Ein Haus WOBA was constituted in July 2017. The Wohngenossenschaft Eglisee handed it the house, empty since spring 2017, for restoration and subletting to two students (association's site).
funding_verdict: Ein Haus WOBA: donor-funded: foundations, companies, a cooperative and private donors

name: Kaskadenkondensator (Kasko)
overview: Self-managed project space for contemporary art, performance and art mediation in the Werkraum Warteck pp, in the Wettsteinquartier near the Rhine in Basel (Kasko info page).

Founded in 1994 as an association. The founding members included the artists Renée Levi, Renate Buser and Marianne Schuppe. The venue is in the Werkraum Warteck pp, a former brewery (German Wikipedia).
Space: it operates within the Werkraum Warteck pp. The Kasko info page says the space was being renovated in 2021 and the website relaunched.
funding_verdict: Kaskadenkondensator (Kasko): costs covered by state contributions from the Canton of Basel-Stadt, foundations and occasional rental income; supporters GGG Basel and Christoph Merian Stiftung

name: Schaulager
overview: Art storage building, museum and research institute at Ruchfeldstrasse 19, Münchenstein, just outside Basel. Tram 11 from Basel SBB station stops at "Schaulager" in about 10 minutes (museenbasel.ch).

Completed in 2003, built under commission of the Laurenz Foundation. It holds the Emanuel Hoffmann Foundation collection, started in 1933 by Maja Hoffmann-Stehlin, later Maja Sacher (archiweb.cz, Wikipedia).
A hybrid of storage facility and museum, built to hold parts of the collection that are normally not visible to the public (archiweb.cz).
funding_verdict: Schaulager: privately funded: the Laurenz Foundation of Maja Oeri

press_items.title: Petr Šmídek, commentary on the Schaulager building (undated)

name: Kunstmuseum Bern
overview: Fine art museum at Hodlerstrasse 8 to 12 in Bern, about 10 minutes on foot from Bern station (museum website).
Established in 1879 (Wikipedia). Its holdings run from the Middle Ages to the present and include works by Paul Klee, Pablo Picasso and Ferdinand Hodler.

In May 2014 the museum was named sole heir of the collector Cornelius Gurlitt, whose homes held more than 1,400 artworks, many suspected of being stolen from European Jews by the Nazis. The bequest required provenance research, and the board voted to accept it in November 2014 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Kunstmuseum Bern: a public funding body and foundations, with UBS as main sponsor
wider_context: FinCEN announced on 3 August 2026 a $125 million penalty against UBS Financial Services Inc. for willful violations of the Bank Secrecy Act. The release concerns anti-money laundering failures, including more than 50,000 foreign currency wires worth more than $10 billion that were inadequately monitored, not sanctions violations. The penalty is against the US subsidiary, not UBS, the sponsor the museum names.

The Federal Reserve announced on 10 May 2004 that UBS AG of Zurich consented to a $100 million civil money penalty "in connection with U.S. dollar banknote transactions with counterparties in jurisdictions subject to sanctions under U.S. law", naming Cuba, Libya, Iran and Yugoslavia. The order is against UBS AG; the museum's partner page lists UBS.
UBS is the museum's main sponsor (museum partner page).

name: Villa Le Lac
overview: A house on Lake Geneva at Route de Lavaux 21 in Corseaux, a 20-minute walk from Vevey station (villa's site), with 64 m² of floor area (English Wikipedia).
Le Corbusier built it in 1923 according to the villa's chronology. English Wikipedia gives 1923 to 1924 and names Pierre Jeanneret as co-designer and Le Corbusier's parents as the clients.
The Fondation Le Corbusier, created in 1968, has owned the villa since 1971. The Association Villa "Le Lac" Le Corbusier has run the museum since 1 January 2013 (villa's site).
funding_verdict: Villa Le Lac: association-run: Commune de Corseaux, unnamed foundations, companies and individuals, and admission; the Fondation Le Corbusier owns and maintains it

name: Haus Duldeck (Rudolf Steiner Archiv)
overview: Reinforced-concrete house at Rüttiweg 15 on the Goetheanum hill in Dornach. The Rudolf Steiner Archive has occupied it since 2002 (Archive's house page).
Rudolf Steiner designed it with the architect Hermann Ranzenberger. The project began in September 1913 and construction started in February 1915 (Archive's house page).
Steiner had it built as thanks to the Grosheintz family, who donated most of the land for the first Goetheanum (Archive's house page).
funding_verdict: Rudolf Steiner Nachlassverwaltung: donor and grant funded foundation: project grants, donations and rent
wider_context: Sven Ove Hansson, "Anthroposophy and Racism" (Aura: Journal for the Study of New Religions, vol. 14, 2025): concludes that Steiner and many leading followers persistently promoted ideas about race that resemble white supremacist ideas, and examines the movement's defences. The abstract read does not name the Archive or Haus Duldeck.
The Archive edits and publishes Steiner's works; its 2025 project grants and donations of CHF 1,393,365 paid for archive and edition work (annual report 2025).

name: National Museum of Damascus
overview: National archaeology museum on Shukri al-Quwatli Street, west of the city centre, between Damascus University and the Sulaymaniyya Takiyya (English Wikipedia). Arabic name: al-Mathaf al-Watani bi-Dimashq (المتحف الوطني بدمشق; romanisation ours).
Founded in 1919, during King Faisal's Arab Kingdom of Syria, under the Ministry of Education at the Al-Adiliyah Madrasa; Wikipedia calls it the oldest cultural heritage institution in Syria.

Building: the present building went up in 1936 beside the Sulaymaniyya Takiyya, with a facade made from the front walls of the Umayyad desert palace Qasr al-Hayr al-Gharbi; the official opening was in 1950, and a three-storey wing for Islamic-period and contemporary Syrian art was added in 1953 (English Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: National Museum of Damascus: public: Syria's Directorate-General of Antiquities and Museums, with a UNESCO emergency project from 2025

name: TheCube Project Space
overview: Independent non-profit art space in the Gongguan and Shida area of Taipei, on the 2nd floor of No. 13, Lane 1, Lane 136, Section 4, Roosevelt Road, behind the east side of Shui Yuan Market and a short walk from Gongguan MRT Station Exit 1 (the space's about page).
Founded in April 2010. It is registered as a non-profit organisation under Taipei's performing arts group regulations. The Chinese name is 立方計劃空間 (the space's about page).

Mission: to promote contemporary art and in-depth humanities thinking, connect international and local networks and engage with art history, through exhibitions, talks, exchange and archival resources (the space's about page).
funding_verdict: TheCube Project Space: public and private grants plus crowdfunding: National Culture and Arts Foundation, Taipei City Department of Cultural Affairs, a foundation and an individual donor

name: National Museum of Tajikistan
overview: National history and art museum at Ismoili Somoni Street 11, next to State Flag Square in central Dushanbe (Eurasia.Travel; Tajik public procurement register). Tajik name Osorkhonai Millii Tojikiston (Осорхонаи миллии Тоҷикистон), Russian Natsionalnyy muzey Tadzhikistana (Национальный музей Таджикистана) (English Wikipedia).

Founded in 1934 with 530 items from the Tajik SSR Academy of Sciences and expeditions; it was named for the miniaturist Kamoliddin Behzad, was renamed the National Museum of Tajikistan in 2011 and moved to its present building in March 2013 (Eurasia.Travel).

An undated Orexca description of the earlier Behzod museum says it was set up by decree of the All-Russian Central Executive Committee in 1934 on the basis of an economic achievements exhibition, gained national status by government decision in 1999, worked from the 1960s in a former technical college building, and gave its third floor to Tajik history and the work of President Emomali Rahmon (translation ours).
funding_verdict: National Museum of Tajikistan: public: a Tajik state institution set up by presidential decree

name: Dar Foto Festival
overview: Annual photography festival in Dar es Salaam with exhibitions, portfolio reviews, street and documentary photo walks and talks with professionals (PH Museum).
Founded by the Tanzanian photographer Andrew Stephen Munuwa, its Creative Director; the German photographer and curator Valentin Rudloff has been co-founder since 2023 (Humboldt Forum; The Citizen).

The festival's own About page said Munuwa founded it in 2021 in the living room of his home in South Dar es Salaam (festival website, archive copy of April 2025); the Humboldt Forum gives 2020 and The Citizen says it launched in 2023.
funding_verdict: Dar Foto Festival: founder-led and self-produced through Tanzania Foto Collective Company Limited

name: MOCA Bangkok
overview: Privately owned five-floor museum of contemporary art at 499 Kamphaeng Phet 6 Road, Lat Yao, Chatuchak, Bangkok. The Sawasdee guide says the Bang Khen station of the SRT Red Line serves it.

Founded by the telecoms executive Boonchai Bencharongkul. Wikipedia gives the opening as 23 March 2012 and says it was previously called the Art Centre. His son Kanachai runs it (Sawasdee, 2022). Lux (1 December 2023) calls the son a co-owner and says the father has not fully handed over control.
Not named for a person.
funding_verdict: MOCA Bangkok: self-funded: the founder's own money
wider_context: The Nation, "Foundation chaired by Boonchai's sister implicated in KCUC embezzlement probe" (16 June 2017): Boonchai's younger sister, Wanna Chirakiti, chairs the Khun Yay Maha Ratana Upasika Chandra Khonnokyoong Foundation, which is under the patronage of the monk Phra Dhammachayo, who faced an arrest warrant on money-laundering charges. Thailand's Department of Special Investigation summoned her several times. A special prosecutor said the foundation built temple facilities with money from Supachai Srisupa-aksorn, who was jailed for stealing from the Klongchan cooperative. The article does not say what she was asked or whether she was charged.
The special prosecutor said in the same article: "to date there has been no evidence that Boonchai was involved in alleged money-laundering." The article does not describe any donations by Boonchai.
Wikipedia says Boonchai follows the Dhammakaya movement.

name: MAIIAM
overview: Private contemporary art museum at 122 Moo 7, Tonpao, San Kamphaeng District, about 20 minutes from central Chiang Mai (museum website).

Founded by Jean Michel Beurdeley and Patsri Bunnag (called late by ArtAsiaPacific), with their son Eric Bunnag Booth. ASEF Culture360 gave its opening date as 3 July 2016 (museum website; ASEF Culture360, 17 June 2016).
Named for Chao Chom Iam, a royal consort to King Rama V and Booth's great-great-aunt (museum website).
funding_verdict: MAIIAM: private: a collector initiative sharing the founding family's collection

name: Chora Museum (Kariye)
overview: Former Byzantine monastery church of St Saviour in Chora in the Edirnekapı neighbourhood of Fatih, Istanbul, outside the Theodosian walls; since 2020 it is the Kariye Mosque (Daily Sabah; Bianet).
Built as a monastery in 534; most of the present building dates from 1077 to 1081, and Theodore Metochites renovated and extended it between 1316 and 1321 (Bianet; Daily Sabah).
Made a mosque in 1511 under Sultan Bayezid II's grand vizier Atık Ali Paşa; a museum by a Council of Ministers decree in 1945, opened to the public in 1958 (Bianet).
funding_verdict: Chora (Kariye): state: owned by the Ministry of Culture and Tourism's General Directorate of Foundations, used for worship under the Presidency of Religious Affairs
wider_context: In May 2024 Greek prime minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said he would raise his "strong dissatisfaction" with Erdoğan, and the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of New York urged Turkey to reconsider (The Art Newspaper, 2024).
In 2005 the Association of Permanent Foundations and Service to Historical Artifacts and Environment sued to end the museum status (Bianet).
In 2020 Erdoğan dropped plans to pray in person at Chora after UNESCO warned that unilateral changes to Chora and Hagia Sophia could affect their World Heritage standing (The Art Newspaper, 2024).

Erdoğan's 2020 prayers at Hagia Sophia drew an outcry from Russia, the EU, the US, Pope Francis and Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew; the Chora decree followed Hagia Sophia's by a month (The Art Newspaper, 2020 and 2024).

press_items.title: Ayla Jean Yackley, "Turkey reopens former Byzantine Chora church as a mosque amid muted objections" (2024)
Gareth Harris, "First Hagia Sophia, now Turkey's 'Sistine Chapel of Byzantium' will be turned back into mosque" (2020)
Merih Danalı Cantarella and Anthony Cutler, "The Kariye Museum in Istanbul: a Byzantine masterpiece under threat" (2020)

name: Barjeel Art Foundation
overview: A foundation that keeps and lends a collection of art from the Arab world, with offices in Muwailih, Sharjah, and a long-term display, 'Parallel Histories', in a wing of the Sharjah Art Museum (foundation website).

Sultan Sooud Al Qassemi, a member of Sharjah's ruling family who began collecting in 2003 and co-founded Meem Gallery in Dubai in 2007, established the foundation in Sharjah in 2010 (Apollo, 7 September 2017).

The collection held 1,800 works in May 2024, of modern and contemporary Arab art with a stress on forgotten Arab modernists and women artists; nearly 100 works were then out on loan and 122 hung at the Sharjah Art Museum, 68 by women and 54 by men (The Art Newspaper, 14 May 2024). The foundation's online collection lists 1,513 artworks, searchable by artist, country and medium (foundation website).
funding_verdict: Barjeel Art Foundation: private, the founder's collection; no funder or amount stated

name: The Bowes Museum
overview: Art museum in a French-style chateau at Newgate, Barnard Castle, County Durham, set in landscaped gardens (Wikipedia).

Founded by John Bowes and his wife Joséphine Benoîte Coffin-Chevallier, Countess of Montalbo. Both died before it opened. Construction began in 1869 and the museum opened to the public in June 1892 (Wikipedia; History of Parliament).
Named for John Bowes. Joséphine was a French actress and painter whom he married in 1852 and who died in 1874 (History of Parliament).
funding_verdict: The Bowes Museum: mainly grants and earned income: Arts Council England and Durham County Council core funding, plus lottery, trust and charity grants, a cafe and shop
